planting.note: Plant tuberous divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich woodland soil in partial to full shade, in a spot that can be left undisturbed through its summer dormancy.

directions: This is the naturally occurring pink-flowered color form of rue anemone, found scattered among the more common white-flowered populations across its eastern North American woodland range rather than being a bred garden cultivar. Unlike the sterile double-flowered selections sold under names like 'Cameo,' the simple single flowers of this form set seed normally and the plant can slowly self-sow into a drift alongside trilliums and other spring ephemerals. Foliage and flowers emerge together in early spring from small clustered tuberous roots, then the whole plant disappears by early summer, so interplant it with later-emerging ferns or hostas to cover the gap. Grow it exactly as the wild species, in humus-rich, evenly moist woodland soil under deciduous shade.

planting.note: Plant dormant bulbs in late summer to fall, 4-5 inches deep, in humus-rich, well-drained soil under high deciduous shade or at a woodland edge.

directions: This Kyushu-native variety of the Japanese red spider lily carries deeper vermilion-orange flowers than the more typical salmon-pink coloring of the species, clustered in small umbels atop bare summer scapes that emerge well before the strap-like foliage appears in fall. Like other Lycoris, it follows a hysteranthous cycle: leaves emerge after flowering, persist through winter, and die back by late spring, leaving the ground bare until the sudden summer bloom. Site it at a lightly shaded woodland margin among later-emerging perennials or ferns that can mask its leafless dormant season, and leave clumps undisturbed for years to build flowering size.

planting.note: Plant tubers flat-side down, 1-2 inches deep, in fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil under deciduous shade where summer irrigation is minimal.

directions: Native to beech and mixed forest understories of the Caucasus and adjacent northern Turkey, this subspecies of winter cyclamen is generally more cold-hardy than the Mediterranean nominate form and tends toward broader, more rounded, often plain or faintly patterned leaves rather than heavily silvered marbling. It blooms from midwinter into early spring with the same swept-back magenta-pink flowers typical of the species, held just above the emerging foliage. Grow it exactly as C. coum, in gritty, humus-rich soil that drains well in winter, allowing the tuber to go fully dormant and dry over summer. It is still mostly found through specialist alpine and bulb nurseries rather than general garden centers.
sources: Grey-Wilson, Cyclamen: A Guide for Gardeners, Horticulturists and Botanists

planting.note: Plant tubers just below the surface in very well-drained, lean, gritty, alkaline soil in full sun to part shade; best grown where summers are hot and dry.

directions: This subspecies comes from the drier, more continental limestone hills of central and southern Anatolia rather than the Aegean coasts and islands typical of nominate Cyclamen graecum, giving it slightly better tolerance of hot, dry summers and occasional sharper winter cold. It flowers in early autumn before the leaves, producing the same reflexed, rose-pink shuttlecock blooms with a darker basal blotch, followed by handsomely silver-zoned, often velvety dark green leaves through winter. Like the species it needs sharp winter drainage and a baking-dry summer dormancy to thrive, making it best suited to a raised bed, rock garden, or container in climates with summer rainfall. Source tubers only from a specialist cyclamen or alpine nursery, as this subspecies is uncommon in general cultivation.
sources: Grey-Wilson, Cyclamen: A Guide for Gardeners, Horticulturists and Botanists

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in part to full shade under deciduous trees or shrubs.

directions: A European woodland native, this variegated selection of wood melick forms low, loose, slowly creeping tufts of narrow leaves striped cream to white, brightening shady spots where most grasses struggle. Airy, open sprays of small nodding flowers rise just above the foliage in late spring, adding a light textural accent rather than a bold display. It spreads gently by short rhizomes to knit together as a woodland-floor groundcover among hellebores, ferns, and spring bulbs, and tolerates the dry shade and root competition typical under established trees better than most variegated grasses. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth begins.

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light open shade; one of the few ornamental grasses that remains presentable at a woodland edge.

directions: Native to open woodlands and hillsides of Siberia, China, Japan, and Korea, frost grass forms upright clumps of broad, bamboo-like leaves held on slender stems, giving it a softer, more horizontal texture than most upright feather or switch grasses. Airy, purplish-silver seed heads open in late summer above the foliage, and the whole plant takes on striking orange, red, and purple fall tones that persist into winter, hence the common name. It tolerates light, high shade at a woodland edge better than most ornamental grasses, though flowering and fall color are most pronounced with at least a half-day of sun. Spreading slowly outward by short rhizomes, it is easy to divide in spring if a clump needs to be controlled or propagated.
